US EQUITY VIEWS
More Al capex at the expense of buybacks
We forecast S&P 500 cash spending will grow by +21% in 2026 and by +13% in 2026. Capex of \$2 trillion and share buybacks of \$1 trillion will represent the largest uses of cash. For most S&P 500 companies, solid cash flow growth and healthy balance sheets will support solid cash spending growth. However, persistent uncertainty will weigh on cash spending on the margin.
n The AI investment boom will drive a continued shift from buybacks to capex for the S&P 500. Consensus estimates show the largest AI hyperscalers spending \$755 billion on capex in 2026 (+83% year/year), which would represent 100% of their cash flows from operations. These companies have also reduced buybacks, which fell by -64% year/year for the group during 1Q. We forecast S&P 500 capex will grow by +33% in 2026 alongside just +3% growth in gross buybacks. The outlook for AI hyperscaler capex growth in 2027 remains highly uncertain, but our base case remains for continued growth at a decelerating pace.
M&A activity has remained resilient despite elevated uncertainty. Strategic US acquirors have announced nearly \$700 billion in M&A YTD, 140% higher than at the same point in 2025. We forecast the cash component of completed M&A will increase by +80% in 2026 and by +15% in 2027 for S&P 500 companies.

The Q1 earnings season highlighted the ongoing rotation from buybacks to capex and R&D. S&P 500 capex growth is tracking at +39% during Q1 compared with +1% for S&P 500 gross buybacks. Our forecasts imply a continuation of these shifting cash spending priorities. We forecast 55% of cash spending will be allocated towards capex and R&D in 2027 compared with 35% to buybacks and dividends. Goldman Sachs US Equity Views 2 7 May 2026

For the average S&P 500 company, solid cash flow growth will drive solid cash spending growth. In our macro models, earnings growth is generally the most important driver of growth in each use of cash. According to consensus estimates, the median S&P 500 company should grow earnings by a solid 10% in 2026 and 11% in 2027. Consensus expects aggregate S&P 500 EPS will grow even faster (+22% in 2026 and +15% in 2027). However, these estimates are boosted by the largest stocks and some idiosyncratic factors that may not necessarily translate into uniform cash spending growth.
The aggregate S&P 500 cash spending figures will be impacted by the spending priorities of the AI hyperscalers. The large public AI hyperscalers (AMZN, GOOGL, META, MSFT, ORCL) accounted for 34% of S&P 500 capex and R&D compared with 10% of S&P 500 buybacks and dividends in 2025. Consensus expects the hyperscalers to spend \$755 billion on capex in 2026, representing growth of 83%. The outlook for capex growth in 2027 remains uncertain, but we expect a deceleration in the pace of growth.
Increased hyperscaler capex has come at the expense of buybacks, which fell by 64% year/year for the group during 1Q. The hyperscalers now allocate 20% of total spending to buybacks and dividends compared with an average of 34% from 2017-2022. We expect minimal hyperscaler buyback growth through 2027. Consensus estimates show hyperscaler capex amounting to 100% of cash flows from operations this year, which in turn leaves little room to return cash to shareholders without a sharp deceleration in capex growth, a large drawdown of cash balances, or a major increase in debt. Some of the buyback headwind from the hyperscalers will likely be offset by increased buyback activity among the beneficiaries of that capex, such as semiconductor firms.

Both hyperscaler and broader corporate balance sheets remain relatively healthy despite a pickup in debt issuance. Hyperscaler net debt has increased from \$69 billion at the start of 2025 to \$206 billion today. However, net debt relative to EBITDA equals just 0.3x, suggesting ample capacity for debt issuance if they believe the capex opportunity is attractive. For the broader S&P 500, net leverage for the median S&P 500 stock ranks in the 87th percentile since 1985, but interest coverage equals 8x (62nd percentile) and much of S&P 500 debt is fixed rate maturing beyond 2028. Looking forward, our credit strategists expect heavy supply in credit markets in 2026 and modestly widening spreads given the AI build-out and strong M&A-related debt financing.
However, persistently high policy uncertainty poses a marginal headwind to cash spending for the average stock. Uncertainty related to tariffs has largely been replaced with uncertainty related to commodities and supply chains. The Economic Policy

Capex and R&D
We forecast S&P 500 capex will grow by +33% in 2026 and +22% in 2027, driven primarily by the AI hyperscalers. The five largest AI hyperscalers – AMZN, GOOGL, META, MSFT, ORCL – accounted for 32% of S&P 500 capex in 2025. We separately estimate nominal capex for the hyperscalers, the S&P 500 Energy sector, and the S&P 500 ex-Energy to arrive at our aggregate S&P 500 capex forecast.
Excluding Energy and AI hyperscalers, we forecast capex will grow by +9% in 2026 and +8% in 2027. We model capex growth as a function of earnings growth, policy uncertainty, and financial conditions. Solid earnings growth and easy financial conditions will more than offset elevated policy uncertainty. The index will also benefit from secular investments in power even excluding Energy and the AI hyperscalers. During 1Q earnings season, the median S&P 500 company grew capex by +8% year/year. Our economists’ capex tracker also points to solid growth, with the soft data component at +5% and the hard data component at +7% during April.
Consensus expects Energy capex growth will be relatively muted, but the recent rise in energy prices could lead to a capex response in 2027 and beyond. On the back of higher oil prices, analysts have revised Energy cash flows higher. However, their estimates imply the benefit will be relatively short-lived. Consensus estimates imply Energy sector cash flow from operations growth of +29% in 2026 but just +1% growth in 2027. As a result, analysts estimates assume a relatively small capex response, with Energy capex growing by +5% in 2026 and 0% in 2027.
Consensus expects the AI hyperscalers will spend \$755 billion on capex in 2026. Analysts lifted 2026 capex estimates for the group by more than \$90 billion during 1Q earnings season. Part of the upward capex revisions reflects the increase in component costs, such as memory. Microsoft stated “for calendar year 2026, we expect to invest roughly \$190 billion in capital expenditures, which includes approximately \$25 billion from the impact of higher component pricing.” Meta raised its 2026 capex range by \$10 billion, noting it “reflects our expectations for higher component pricing this year and, to a lesser extent, additional data center costs to support future year capacity.” We believe the balance of risks to these estimates is tilted further to the upside, given managements have emphasized the inability of supply to keep pace with demand.

Hyperscaler capex in 2027 remains a large source of uncertainty, but we expect the growth rate will likely decelerate. Hyperscaler capex in 2026 is on track to reach 100% of hyperscaler cash flows from operations. For 2027 capex growth to match 2026 capex growth, the hyperscalers would need to spend roughly \$1.4 trillion on capex. Consensus estimates that cash flows from operations for these companies will equal \$980 billion. Without sharp upward revisions to hyperscaler cash flow growth, these companies would need to increase net debt by \$400 billion. We expect incremental debt issuance among the group but ultimately expect a deceleration in the pace of capex growth.

We expect S&P 500 R&D will grow by +18% in 2026 and by +10% in 2027. In our macro model, sales growth is the primary driver of R&D growth. The median S&P 500 company is forecast to grow sales by +7% in 2026 and +6% in 2027. We also account for the fact that R&D is heavily concentrated in a few large TMT and Health Care firms, where idiosyncratic spending will likely drive R&D growth that is stronger than implied by our macro model. The top 10 stocks account for more than half of S&P 500 R&D and consensus expects they will grow R&D by +27% in 2026 and 12% in 2027.

Buybacks
We forecast S&P 500 gross buybacks will grow by +3% in 2026 and +5% in 2027. We model annual S&P 500 buyback growth as a function of earnings growth, valuation, policy uncertainty, and financial conditions. Historically, earnings growth has been the most important driver of buyback growth. However, rising equity valuations, higher policy uncertainty, and tighter borrowing conditions have contributed to relatively weak growth in buybacks in recent quarters. Data from the GS Buybacks Desk suggest volumes YTD are tracking at 1.1x the level of 2025 activity.
Source: Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research
Reduced buyback activity among the hyperscalers will weigh on aggregate S&P 500 buybacks. Hyperscaler capex has come at the expense of buybacks, which fell by 64% year/year during 1Q. The group now allocates 15% of total cash spending on buybacks compared with an average of 27% from 2017-2022. We expect hyperscaler buyback growth will likely stagnate through 2027. With all of cash flows from operations expected to be allocated towards capex, it leaves less room to return cash to shareholders without a sharp deceleration in capex growth, a drawdown of cash balances, or an increase in debt.
Increased buybacks from Banks and the beneficiaries of AI capex, such as semis, should help offset some of those headwinds. NVDA and AVGO have generated extremely strong cash flow growth and have started to repurchase more stock. They bought back \$52 billion in 2025, compared with \$40 billion in 2024. NVDA authorized a \$60 billion buyback program in late 2025 and AVGO authorized a \$10 billion program this year. Financials represent one quarter of S&P 500 buybacks and appear poised for further growth.

Dividends We forecast S&P 500 dividends will grow by +6% in 2026 and +5% in 2027. We model dividend growth as a function of earnings growth in the concurrent year and in each of the two years prior. Solid EPS growth should support modest dividend increases. Through the first four months of the year, S&P 500 DPS grew by 6.6% year/year. We forecast +5% annualized DPS growth over the next 10 years. We forecast +6% annualized EPS growth over the next 10 years. Our DPS estimates imply a further decline in the dividend payout ratio to roughly 25%, in part due to the rising popularity of buybacks.

Cash M&A
Despite a challenging macro backdrop, US M&A activity has been strong. Strategic US acquirors have announced nearly \$700 billion in M&A YTD, 140% higher than at the same point in 2025. Sponsor M&A growth has been weaker, totaling \$190 billion (-37% year/year).
We forecast completed cash M&A for the S&P 500 will grow by +80% in 2026 and +15% in 2027. From a macro perspective, M&A activity will be supported by resilient CEO confidence, solid US economic growth, and relatively easy financial conditions. M&A will also benefit from the combination of a friendly regulatory backdrop and a desire for AI-related business transformation. Our forecast for completed M&A is sensitive to the closing timelines of a few large deals that have already been announced.
The cash component of M&A activity has remained close to recent averages despite high equity valuations. Companies historically have shifted towards share-based compensation when valuations are elevated. However, cash has represented nearly 70% of announced M&A deal value YTD.
